Horrible public key tricks

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.

... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4"

There is prior art of protest SSL implementations, but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.

The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be week, no one would know unless they actually try to break it.

# openssl s_client -connect maurycyz.com:443 < /dev/null 2> /dev/null \ | sed -n /BEGIN/,/END/p | grep -zE '////.?*////' --color=yes -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIFADCCA+igAwIBAgISBjst/cQvgUTu+O7siJYo8bAFMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBCwUA MDMxCzAJBgNVBAYTAlVTMRYwFAYDVQQKEw1MZXQncyBFbmNyeXB0MQwwCgYDVQQD EwNZUjIwHhcNMjYxMTA4MjE0NzM5WhcNMjcwMjA2MjE0NzM4WjAXMRUwEwYDVQQD EwxtYXVyeWN5ei5jb20wggEiMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBAQUAA4IBDwAwggEKAoIBAQCz lkaPgD2IZPPtC6fB////You+dont+actually+have+to+pick+random+privat e+keys//No+one+checks+these+things//A+certificate+aurthority+got +away+with+the+number+4+for+a+year////8HzhFiAzSv/zKHf7l4u6d6d3w6 nOg7N/C2ra5QvNpFnZVzrS5IcZmvRdi0dcptavcB8s4ThHNZLhY414Mvdo5t0kr0 n8WFrydnc6NEMKDPiZxehnF5D3n7z1piI5YCsNcS0NVFb45+8QvBZrv0O2BSIKNE 7M9hcE00KsaSzZ3eDBsRAgMBAAGjggIoMIICJDAOBgNVHQ8BAf8EBAMCBaAwEwYD VR0lBAwwCgYIKwYBBQUHAwEwDAYDVR0TAQH/BAIwADAdBgNVHQ4EFgQUZoonXxel KC563vN2kbvwXTLBQgMwHwYDVR0jBBgwFoAUQBUtJnntMiCe35pyHdYyH4EMgQww MwYIKwYBBQUHAQEEJzAlMCMGCCsGAQUFBzAChhdodHRwOi8veXIyLmkubGVuY3Iu b3JnLzAnBgNVHREEIDAegg4qLm1hdXJ5Y3l6LmNvbYIMbWF1cnljeXouY29tMBMG A1UdIAQMMAowCAYGZ4EMAQIBMC0GA1UdHwQmMCQwIqAgoB6GHGh0dHA6Ly95cjIu Yy5sZW5jci5vcmcvNi5jcmwwggELBgorBgEEAdZ5AgQCBIH8BIH5APcAdgAAGl0a HC2TdbZIVXj4L3Ghrm7vOX0pfIrjFXvK3uGgHgAAAaG9Vy0ZAAAEAwBHMEUCIEof iI14E0jzfOz9woGKiiYR4pUAm/Dv9FmFWEr5ma8uAiEAyl2EMpURJ65Oe+FIFE6v Uj4QomzFJ98qVqhQozQxcC4AfQAai51rjdeR0c0FSe22A1XWBrZPrTDbcf54jw/H yPvEsQAAAaG9Vy2AAAgAAAUAFVVRHQQDAEYwRAIgTBocYGR/XcTqNx58xJh/pAme q+w6fDl+NktKUuPBqZcCIFJU6/GE71s9OkORDBC4+XHiQWWxrHk8uuD6nTQzCtHS MA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBCwUAA4IBAQAUIK5MyB3bhSFc6NOkC1UYYi2BQZN4zDfZMTD1 gGtnK7FCCNKvsanv9FIeGgr7e3A50TJhqIWH42uz9mQt8rnofwKVu7fJ77l/HZIf oAqNol06AbtwM2I4vOEAZyfD3zAfL/3G70rGw4omDFpzX852Yi3Ou40wpHbdboYY Bn58bZDvBVaUrKVdTdN+S5Ea2usWKgUjqfouz/VjnlEgLfcxqPwF2IPfPCOPKJH2 uIo3tnjx267OWY3O8nyxuOAxrBuP5fc8g2bEcKI5RewRWh7CCVZB23Ov5dyFQVcb ICN41m494GUBgwqYpAjLgdIubvyoJzBpACGuIl2QlJza1p/y -----END CERTIFICATE-----

First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent.

The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent:

# Encryption requires knowing e (public) cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n

The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q.

# Decryption requires knowing d (pivate) = cyphertext^d mod n = plaintext^e^d mod n = plaintext^(e*d) mod n = plaintext^1 mod n = plaintext

Ok, back to vanity keys. The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there.

The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus.

My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p.

The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product:

58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176 (incrementing until the next prime...) 58174124 * 918491843 = 53432458367670532

As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner.

From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key:

# Single domain openssl req -new -key priv.pem -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request # Wildcard cat > config< cert_request certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request ... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts.

The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated.

Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) avalable charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice.

As for security, this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. I'm not aware of any factoring algorithms that could exploit key selection method, but I can't garantee they don't exist. The method may also produce a p and q that are close together, which makes it possible to easly factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also allow factorisation.

While I wouldn't trust these keys for anything important, they should be perfectly fine for serving a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires man-in-the-middle even if the private key is compromised.

How Much Energy Does Building Distro Packages Use

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

When I set up the infrastructure for Casuarina Linux I repurposed an AMD AM4 system with RyzenÂ 9Â 5950X 16-Core CPU (105W TDP) and 32Gb of DDR4 RAM as the build server. I set it up in our laundry, connected it via a smart plug, and reset its counters. Over the course of the project I would regularly pull package updates from Chimera Linux, build and install them locally, and then push them to the repo, which would trigger Buildbot to build and publish them.

You can select a different currency, which will use exchange rates from the time of writing.

The project ran from 30 March 2026 to 8 November 2026 (a bit over 7 months) the total energy used was 98.4 kWh. My electricity plan is a 100% renewable plan (meaning they offset the non-renewable parts) and costs AU$0.33 kWh. Ignoring the daily service fee the cost of that electricity is AU$32.47 .

Since it turned out I was the only one doing package updates I kept the builder off when idle. When there were packages to build Iâd hit the power button (on the machine, not the smart plug) and some time later when it was done it press it again to shut it down. This was pretty beneficial as the idle draw was about 55W.

The number of package builds was around 5000. SELECT COUNT(name) FROM logs WHERE name LIKE 'pkg:%'; from the Buildbot state.sqlite yields 5201, however thatâs probably slightly inflated due to rebuilds/packages that failed to build on the first try.

The actual usage is likely more than double the 98kWh figure as all packages were built on my desktop machine first, before pushing to the repository for the builder to pick up. That machine is an AM5 system with AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-Core CPU (170W TDP), 64Gb DDR5 RAM. Additionally our house has rooftop solar, and where possible I would kick off builds during the day so there was a better chance of using the solar. That would have reduced the actual cost, but I have no way to measure the specific amount.

The slowest package by far to build was Chromium, taking just shy of 4 hours to complete. Power draw measured by the smart plug when the builder was fully loaded is about 193W. So 4 hours at 193W is 0.77kWh, which means a Chromium build costs about 25 cents.

Overall it cost a bit under AU$5 a month (ignoring solar, and my workstation) to build all the packages for a Linux distribution. Thatâs not too bad I think.

InfoQ Homepage Articles Agentic AI Architecture: Current Challenges and Future Opportunities

Nov 09, 2026 11 min read

Most software engineers and architects are innately familiar with microservices and cloud-native architectures and have been involved in building systems based on these architectures for many years. Microservice-based systems tend to consist of tens or hundreds, and sometimes even thousands of services, responsible for different types of data processing, be it API endpoints, data pipelines, back-office workflows, and anything in between, but they do have one thing in common - they merely process data using a logic determined either by code or based on data retrieved from data stores. This doesn’t mean that such systems are simplistic - far from it. Still, despite their complexity, they can be reasoned about deterministically, which helps define and scope functionality, implement and test changes, and operate such systems, even in the face of infrastructure- or application-level failures.

All of this is about to change. Indeed, a good share of future software systems will still be deterministic and resemble what we are used to today. Still, quite soon, swathes of IT systems being designed and delivered will be leveraging AI-based solutions to power user-facing functionality. For most, if not all, architects and engineers, this will require significant adaptation to the new reality of the IT industry.

Automated code transformation at scale. Fix vulnerabilities, migrate frameworks, and modernize legacy code across every repo. Try Moderne Free.

The adoption of AI in software architectures is driven primarily by the new capabilities that it offers, which are particularly useful for products used by knowledge workers. Historically, IT systems focused on storing, processing, and making data available via APIs and user interfaces. At the same time, humans were responsible for a good portion of data administration, utilizing business rules, procedures, office "tribal" knowledge, and their own judgment. It’s fair to point out that some, or even much, of this intelligence was built directly into IT systems to improve productivity, particularly when scaling business operations was critical. With AI-enabled capabilities, software systems can shift from operating on raw data to knowledge, thereby elevating IT's role from merely a data management and processing function to knowledge-level support for business operations and end-user functionality.

It’s difficult to gauge to what extent AI-based solutions will dominate next-generation software systems. Still, by all signs, the impact will be so substantial that we can speak about a new type of software architecture, one where AI powers large areas of functionality, making humans using products built on top of next-generation systems much more productive. Agentic AI Architecture is a software architecture in which agentic AI systems are leveraged on a substantial scale, geared towards making optimal use of generative AI (and other) models. This type of architecture builds on microservices and cloud-native architecture and adds agentic AI capabilities.

Agentic AI isn’t exactly new, but equally, it’s not yet well established either. Over the last couple of years, agentic AI systems have evolved from simple, single-agent solutions to chains, to graphs and multi-agent systems (MAS), where multiple agents collaborate, organized in various topologies. This area is still undergoing active development, and more elaborate use cases will inevitably emerge. It’s fair to say, though, that different collaboration strategies or topologies work best for specific use cases, so choosing a simpler solution can be advantageous in many cases.

Agents make the most of the large language models (LLMs) they interact with by providing the right context. Here again, after starting with predefined prompts, the solutions gradually shifted to a dynamic context based on output from other agents, context propagation, or data fetched from external sources via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

As the amount of context accumulated from different sources began to cause problems with diminished reasoning, engineers developed new ways of managing context, and context engineering emerged as a separate practice. The progressive context disclosure technique can further enhance the context preparation step by allowing the agent to selectively load detailed information into the context window based on the user’s prompt.

Since LLMs have effective limits on context size, the role of context engineering is to ensure that the context used maximizes the model's likelihood of producing the desired outcome, or at least minimizes the chance of hallucinations due to vague or inadequate context. Effective context engineering requires context management to store, optimize, and reuse context elements for subsequent agent invocations.

Lately, memory systems for AI agents have also emerged, enabling further enhancements to context editing. These systems organize different types of long-term memory (episodic, semantic, procedural) for storage and querying, thus allowing agents to supplement the context with past experiences/decisions, relevant facts/definitions, rules, or learned behaviors.

Context engineering has become a foundational architectural concern for agentic AI systems. It will undoubtedly continue to evolve as the needs and expectations for building and operating AI-based products grow.

Agentic AI has developed its own specialized set of communications protocols. This process was largely driven by challenges related to the complexity of agent development, the need for standardization, and the need for improved interoperability:

For agentic AI systems to be valuable, they need to be integrated into a bigger enterprise architectures. In the enterprise setting, incorporating an agentic AI system can be done by:

A large-scale enterprise-level architecture may comprise many specialized agentic AI systems. Since AI agents can use MCP to use database, services/APIs or any arbitrary data sources directly, it’s important to ensure that their interactions are constrainted within a bounded context, as defined by the domain-driven design (DDD). Limiting the reach of agentic AI systems within larger architectures reduces coupling between distant or unrelated components and data sources, allowing more cohesive areas to be maintained by engineering teams without excessive dependencies or large blast radius if changes are introduced.

Figure 1: Multiple Agentic AI Systems in Separate Bounded Contexts (Source: created by the author)

Figure 1 (above) depicts somewhat simplified architecture with two bounded context, each one embedding an agentic AI system with multiple agents (A), as well as other microservices (S). Agents only use local data sources and services for context expansion or as tools, hence limiting the coupling with other parts of the boarder software system.

The scalability of cloud-based software architectures is well understood, as architects and engineers have been building and operating them for some time. The same can’t be said for agentic AI systems, where LLM call latencies are higher, and more complex multi-agent systems can further increase processing times. The performance of agentic AI systems can’t be measured solely by standard metrics such as throughput, latency, or error rates.

Researchers at Google and MIT published a paper introducing a framework for scaling multi-agent systems. The team behind the framework tested various multi-agent coordination strategies, each with several configuration parameters, including the number of LLM calls, agents, and interactions per agent. Scientists concluded that the best coordination strategy is task-dependent: financial reasoning does better with centralized orchestration, while web navigation benefits from a decentralized strategy.

The results shared by Google and MIT demonstrate that there is no one-size-fits-all approach when it comes to agentic AI, and teams building complex solutions have to experiment and empirically establish the agent coordination strategy that is best suited to the task.

Incorporating agentic AI into the distributed system architecture significantly alters the security model. Agentic AI contributes additional security threats, particularly around the agent runtime, tool servers (MCP or others), and the model provider. AI agents, for instance, can be susceptible to prompt injection, instruction confusion, or tool output poisoning, leading to unintended actions or leaking data they have access to. Additionally, using external LLM models introduces risks around data residency, retention, or usage.

Furthermore, present access-control models, honed over many decades, are ill-suited to cater to agents, which can’t really be treated as human users or backend services. Cameron Pavey, senior developer at Auth0, recently proposed a new permission model specifically targeting AI agents. He argues that regular (non-AI) backend services are generally more trusted because they are deterministic and auditable, while authentication sessions and user interfaces restrict users. Agents, on the other hand, can arbitrarily trigger multi-step workflows that involve other agents and tool calls without the user’s explicit knowledge or permission.

Pavey proposes using capability-scoped permissions and task-scoped credentials as key steps toward solving the problem of agent permissions and adopting fine-grained authorization systems for layered enforcement.

It’s worth pointing out that this is not the first time that the security landscape has experienced a marked expansion. When microservices and cloud-native architectures entered the scene, we observed a shift in this area as well, leading to a revision of the access control mechanism and protocol and the emergence of now-common technologies such as JWT and OAuth.

Considering the non-deterministic nature of agentic AI systems, observability is key to being able to effectively build, enhance, troubleshoot and operarate them.

Teams should aim at complete coverage across all pillars of modern observability platforms:

Despite the expected rise of agentic AI as the driving force behind future IT products and services, we cannot expect an instant switch. For many years, the distributed systems architectures we know today will coexist with the next-generation ones (which build on top of them), similar to how service-oriented architecture (SOA) was phased out in favor of microservices over a few years.

Additionally, given the relative infancy of agentic AI, this space will take time to mature and gain widespread adoption, allowing for a gradual transition and the emergence of new patterns, best practices, and technologies that will further drive adoption.

Finally, not all products or business processes need to leverage agentic AI, or the use of AI may not be immediately financially viable. It may be that certain industries or classes of products or systems will not benefit from AI at the same pace as others. In that sense, microservices and cloud-native architectures are here to stay in one way or another.

With Agentic AI taking center stage and maturity and adoption within the industry growing, I expect many components and solutions, currently often custom-built, to be offered as features of more generic platforms that will support multi-agent system delivery and operations, as well as the integration of those into broader enterprise-level architectures.

In particular, foundational agentic AI building blocks, such as agent memory, asset registry, guardrails, and orchestration, as well as support for observability and operations, should all become built-in capabilities of agentic AI platforms, whether homegrown or offered by vendors or cloud providers.

There are several agentic AI platforms/frameworks that developers can use today, including LangChain (with LangGraph), CrewAI, Azure AI Foundry, Google Agent SDK (ADK), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.

This process will follow the same path as it did for microservice architectures, where growing needs from organizations adopting these new architectures have necessitated the creation of internal, self-operated solutions that externally hosted and managed products will gradually replace.

The industry is on the verge of a major shift, and Agentic AI Architecture has a strong chance of becoming a dominant architecture for distributed systems over the coming years and decades. This doesn’t mean that microservices and cloud-native architectures will become obsolete; rather, they will form the basis of the next generation of systems, in which AI powers much of the user experience. What architects and engineers are familiar with today will form a foundation for delivering robust AI-powered products and services that combine data, knowledge, and compute-based reasoning.

The shift described here will increase productivity and improve ease of use for many knowledge workers across many sectors. It will greatly reshape not only the IT industry but our entire modern society.

While we are still in the early days, with a lot of innovation, moving goalposts, experimentation, and learning, we can certainly expect an exciting road ahead.

Edoardo Vacchi: No, no, it is correct on a high level. More specifically, so VLLM is our inference engine. So, you can think of it, if you will, as the JVM of language models. So, it has support for several language models, there's an interesting aside here, it is a platform to run LLMs. The interesting aside here is you would expect that this is a general sort of VM, and the LLMs are sort of software that you load on top of it. But unfortunately every LLM architecture is slightly different. So, VLLM has to basically include the implementation of every LLM that gets released. So, when people release LLMs, they do not release the software to run them, they release the weights. So, all of these inference engines, such as VLLM, what they do is implementing basically the software, the kernels, the components that actually load the weights and then actually do the inference.

So, VLLM is our platform to run the core and effectively VLLM is able to serve, it's a server... I mean, it's an inference engine, it's also server that exposes endpoints that you can call to do inference, and it does so efficiently. It was originally VLLM, I think the V in VLLM originally stands for virtual, as in virtual memory allocation. Because it was the first engine to implement page detention, basically a mechanism inspired by good old systems programming to do paging of memory, memory pages, but for memory that gets allocated on GPU, this is in a very high level way. So, VLLM is able to do high throughput inference. So, you can do several requests at once and VLLM will pack them and try to serve them together, and do inference in one pass for several requests at one time, this is called continuous batching. But this gets you to a point.

Essentially, at some point you have your GPUs on your machine, and your inference engine and that's it. You will not be able to scale further than the resources that you have on that machine. So, how do you scale further? Well, you can scale by having more VLLM instances, right? So, you have several VLLM instances and you want to serve your inference requests using these few VLLM, these few VLLM instances that you have. Now, you have another problem. How do you route requests across your VLLM instances? So, if you are on Kubernetes, what you will do... And most people are on Kubernetes these days, it's the standard for platforms for serving services in an efficient way. So, you can scale your VLLM instances and have several VLLM instances that serve the possible the same request... I mean that gets selected by the scheduler, by the VLLM scheduler.

If you do it the traditional way and let the Kubernetes normal router to pick across the VLLM instances that you have replicated, you won't get necessarily good performance. The reason is inference does not behave like a traditional service, a traditional HTP service. Basically, if you send a request to one specific VLLM instance, especially if you are doing conversation, if you're doing a chat and if you're doing agentic coding, it's still a chat basically. There's a lot of exchanges back and forth between you and your server, between your agent and your server. You want to stick for as much time as possible to the same VLLM instance. This might be counterintuitive in a way because for microservices, we know we don't want to hammer the same service on and on because otherwise it will get overloaded. We want to do sort of round robbing or random robbing across the replicas.

But the thing is microservices or service in general, these are usually in a way stateless. The state is usually stored somewhere else and it's not part of your request. I mean, the request can be served independently by any instance. Unfortunately for LLMs, in order for LLMs to do their inference in an efficient way, you want to stick for as much time as possible to the same instance. But at the same time, you cannot stick forever to the same instance because at some point you will reach some limit. You are not the only user of that VLLM instance. You want to serve and distribute the load across your VLLM instances. So there's a balance that you have to strike between staying with the same instance and benefit of the caches, the KV caches, the prefix caches that are in place, the systems that allow you to do inference in an efficient way and lower costs.

But at the same time, you don't want to overload the same instance too much. So you also have to keep this into account. This is not the job for a traditional Kubernetes schedule. And that's where llm-d comes into place. That's what llm-d does. llm-d is not just a router or a scheduler. It's actually a family of projects and they are all meant to give you a set of tools to do distributed inference so that you can leverage all of the GPUs that you have and use it at their maximum as much as possible so you get the best value, the best bang for your bucks because these hardware is expensive whether you loan it or you own it. So you want to use it 100% as much as possible. And that's why we provide scheduler. We have something that we're going to release. I mean, in the open source ecosystem, it's already been released.

We're going to release also as part of product of Red Hat. This is called batch inference. Batch inference is using your cluster even when it's under load. So you can schedule request to do batch processing in the background when your cluster is underused because basically this hardware is so expensive that you want to keep it at 100% all the time. So even when there is no live inference going on, you can schedule batch processing to run when you're sleeping when there's less work to be done live. So that's what llm-d does. It uses your hardware as much as possible so that the money you spend gets you the best value and you do it on your own hardware so you can do inference without leaking data to a third party, which is important these days.

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, it's a complex problem for sure. As I said, one part of the story is that... Well, I mean, if people that are hearing that the audience know how LLM generally work, essentially the stateful nature of the LLM in a way is fake, in that they are really stateless. The way they do inference is that we send them the entire history of a conversation every single time. So, maybe I jumped at-

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, to the conclusion earlier. And I said a lot about prefix caches and KV caches, but yes. So, essentially the way an LLM works is that essentially you always send the entirety of the conversation to the LLM. And what really happens is the LLM completes the conversation. I don't know if people recall how OpenAI and the GPT Lab playground worked a few years ago. Basically, it was the completion API. You wrote a sentence and then the LLM wrote the continuation of that. And the cool thing was that someone discovered if you wrote that prompt as a conversation, as a dialogue with quotes, user says da, da, da, computer says... The LLM will continue the conversation. And that's how ChatGPT basically was born. People notice this, and notice this pattern.

Now, LLMs are being trained with this pattern, but that's how basically originally it work. So, if you think of it this way, every conversation really is a very long prompt to the continuation of that conversation. The way LLM works, you send the history of the conversation and then they continue with the next answer, and then you get back the answer, and then you continue with your answer, and so on, so forth, so on and so forth. If you are using LLMs, you will know that pricing for these things, depending if you're using token-based spend or a subscription... Well, if you're using a subscription, that doesn't really matter. But if you're using token-based pricing, you will know that there's a difference between cached responses and responses.

The reason is, if you don't do a cached response, then you are sending the entire history of your conversation to the LLM. The LLM does not have that conversation in cache, so it will have to do inference on the entire prompt, and that's why that will be particularly expensive. But if you've been going back and forth for a while without long pauses and the cache on the server has not been evicted, then you've been reusing stored cache estate to continue the conversation. That does not mean necessarily that you haven't sent the entire history to the LLM, it just means that even though you are sending the entire history, the history is recognized as part of a prefix of a cache, and so the LLM can compute only the continuation instead of the entire prompt.

So, we have these mechanism for caching in place so that basically LLMs, if the cache exists, can only infer the last few tokens that continue the conversation instead of have to re-compute the entire state from the prompt. llm-d does that for you. So, it maintains this cache both in the form of a KV cache, with one going to the deals how that works, and a prefix cache. And both these caching mechanism allow you to persist the state across the exchanges in your conversation, persist as in volatile memory because these are caches... Usually they're not persistent for a long time. And that's the reason also why you want to stick usually to the same VLLM instance, even though llm-d also gives you ways to move around across instances. It's a lot, we cannot explain how all that works. But in general, llm-d allows you to do this, allows you to have an efficient use and even for stateful conversation of your hardware.

You don't just have expensive GPUs, but you also have to have expensive connection between just GPUs. We're talking about RDMA. So, it doesn't really matter, sometimes you have a very large model that is able to answer every possible question, it might be useful in many situation, of course, but you have also to bring to the table the cost efficiency.

So, you might have specialized models that are trained or fine-tuned on specific domains, and I think that's where we should go where the next thing should be. Because that really brings LLM inference, AI in general, agentic stuff to the people, it allows you to run this stuff on your hardware, with things that are attainable, goals that are attainable, not just super expensive hardware that nobody can afford.

Olimpiu Pop: I think we are adept, let's say teenage years, of what LLMs and AI will mean for the future because everybody's priding themselves on how much horsepowers do our models have. But actually we are stuck in traffic hours and it doesn't actually matter if it's there or not.

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. Teenage years is a good metaphor, I'd say.

Olimpiu Pop: Maybe just to close up with what's on your roadmap. So, version one is out, what's in the next period? So, upcoming months, upcoming years, what's the target for llm-d?

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, I mentioned a few already actually. So, llm-d itself is able to run because on this hardware, you have to use it efficiently, it's able to run very large models, mixer expert models by sharing them across machines. But things that we are experimenting and we are getting more and more refined are this batch inference concepts so you can leverage your hardware more efficiently and use those dead moments in your traffic to serve and do inference, even scheduled inference, without the live interaction, so you can 100% reuse that hardware that you have.

And the other is obviously, as I just mentioned, semantic classification so that you can not just use the right machines, but also use the right model at the right time. For instance, let's say you have a very big model that is expensive to run, and smaller models that are more efficient to run and you can run on hardware that is much cheaper. Depending on the conversation that you're having on the prompt that you're sending, you might want to use the larger model in some situations or the smaller model in some situation. So, these are the things that we are working on currently, there are more, and I cannot even list all of them. But it's an exciting space and I think you're going to see a lot of interesting stuff in the next coming months.

Olimpiu Pop: Okay, thank you for your time.

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Launches TorchNeuron to Run PyTorch Models on AWS Trainium Without Modifications

Nov 09, 2026 2 min read

At the recent PyTorch Conference North America 2026, Amazon introduced TorchNeuron, a native PyTorch backend that enables developers to run existing PyTorch code on AWS Trainium AI chips with virtually no code modifications.

Beyond reducing engineering effort, TorchNeuron allows enterprises to share hardware capacity between training and inference workloads, reallocating resources from inference to training during off-peak hours.

Amazon says that a single configuration change is sufficient to switch hardware, eliminating the need to rewrite and revalidate models when moving to Trainium.

Today, 85% of AI researchers and developers write their code in PyTorch. Until now, the hardware that code could run on was far more limited than the code itself, and expanding to new chips meant rewriting and revalidating work that took months to perfect.

According to the TorchNeuron documentations, when leveraging PyTorch's automatic device detection through torch.accelerator, the only required change is replacing .to('cuda') to .to('neuron'). The backend also natively supports distributed training and PyTorch parallelism APIs, including DDP, FSDP2, DTensor, and others. In addition, TorchNeuron provides native support for Torch streams and events through torch_neuronx.Stream and torch_neuronx.Event.

Amazon Annapurna Labs vice president Colin Brace, who leads the team behind TorchNeuron, emphasized that his team validated the 100,000 most popular models and more than 800 ML architectures to ensure a smooth developer experience when adopting the new backend.

Additionally, TorchNeuron enables developers and researchers to use the Neuron Kernel Interface to develop, optimize, and execute custom operators:

Developers can obtain finer performance control beyond Adaptive Eager and torch.compile by calling performance critical NKI kernels directly in model code to replace sequences of standard PyTorch operations (ATen ops).

Commenting on Amazon's announcement on LinkedId, Liner Notes Consulting CEO Yasuo Maeda noted that:

The real test will be whether developers can achieve competitive performance and total cost of ownership in production. The AI infrastructure race is not just about who builds the best chips. It is also about who makes them easiest to use at scale.

Similarly, user Pratham pratham hightlighted that, while reducing migration friction is important to avoiding accelerator lock-in, the real test lies in workload-specific performance, cost per token, and reproducibility.

Amazon also emphasizes that TorchNeuron has already been adopted by several organizations, including Cartesia, which is using it for voice AI inference, and the Lieber Institute for Brain Development, which explores applications in drug target identification and drug discovery.

AWS TorchNeuron announcement comes on the heels of Google's launch of TorchTPU, its native PyTorch backend for Google's TPU hardware.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

InfoQ Homepage News Cloudflare Develops Public Certificate Authority for Post-Quantum Web Security

Nov 09, 2026 2 min read

Cloudflare has tested Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) as an alternative to traditional certificate chains, reporting 9% faster median performance in a Chrome experiment. The approach batches certificate data into an append-only Merkle tree, letting clients verify certificates with compact inclusion proofs instead of transmitting a full certificate chain. Cloudflare attributed most of the measured improvement to eliminating intermediate certificates; the experiment used classical signatures rather than post-quantum signatures.

Building on the approach covered in InfoQ’s earlier report, Cloudflare describes how landmark-based verification and independent transparency log cosigners support certificate issuance and verification at scale.

The experiment served billions of MTCs to 50% of Chrome Beta 146 for selected domains on Cloudflare’s free plan. Cloudflare wound down the experiment in August 2026 and is developing a public certificate authority (CA) that supports MTC issuance, targeting inclusion in Chrome’s quantum-resistant Root Store in early 2027, subject to evaluation.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince, in a press release, said:

Upgrading the web's security before quantum computers can break it is one of the biggest coordination challenges in the history of the Internet.

Post-quantum cryptography creates scaling challenges for the Web Public Key Infrastructure (Web PKI). According to Cloudflare, post-quantum signatures can be approximately 40 times larger than classical signatures, increasing bandwidth and storage requirements.

MTCs combine certificate issuance with transparency logging. Instead of signing certificates individually, a certificate authority (CA) records certificate data in an append-only Merkle tree and signs a checkpoint. Clients verify certificate inclusion using cryptographic proofs.

Cloudflare uses the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol to validate domain ownership. An independent mirroring cosigner verifies and stores updated tree states, helping detect inconsistent log views and preserve issuance records if the original log becomes unavailable.

MTC issuance and independent log mirroring (Source: Cloudflare Blog Post)

Landmark relative certificates further reduce TLS handshake data. Cloudflare distributes authenticated landmarks to clients, which verify certificate inclusion using cryptographic proofs. Servers must still prove possession of their private keys. In the common case, the handshake transmits one public key, one signature, and an inclusion proof smaller than 1 KB.

Landmark relative certificate verification using pre-distributed tree landmarks. (Source: Cloudflare Blog Post)

Clients may be newly installed, offline, or missing the relevant landmark update. Servers must therefore retain a standalone MTC certificate as a fallback. Cloudflare identifies independent monitoring at production volume, a diverse ecosystem of CAs and cosigners, and browser support as remaining requirements for broader deployment. Alicja Tendaj, Tier 2 Technical Support Specialist at SSL.com, raised questions about revocation and incident handling in response to Cloudflare’s announcement on LinkedIn:

With short validity and trust anchored in a tree head, a lot of the old OCSP and CRL playbook becomes a question of how quickly you can stop including a certificate

Cloudflare’s planned public CA will require evaluation before its MTC issuance can be trusted through Chrome’s quantum-resistant Root Store. The company says production deployment will help determine whether the approach can maintain transparency, interoperability, and availability at Internet scale.

InfoQ Homepage News Google Releases Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics Control, Simulation, and Policy Improvement

Nov 09, 2026 2 min read

Google has released Gemini 4 Argon framing it as a general-purpose physical-reasoning model for robot control, Real2Sim scene construction, multimodal labeling of robot video, and iterative policy improvement, rather than as a single end-effector policy.

In the published prompts, Argon directs a Boston Dynamics Spot through a foot-pedal task after practice in a MuJoCo twin, steers a simpler arm with visual coordinates and HTTP motion primitives, and closes a loop with the Gemini Omni video world model. Real2Sim examples rebuild MuJoCo scenes from teleoperation video; labeling prompts annotate demonstration footage for behavior cloning. Google also reports synthesizing domain-randomized MuJoCo episodes from one RGB photo to fine-tune a vision-language-action policy, citing a rise from 56% to 75% success on the corresponding real setup.

Early practitioner reaction focused on simulation fidelity. Davin YC Dong commented on X:

Google's Argon robotics examples tune simulation twins against contact events as well as visuals. That is the part I'd inspect: a scene can look convincing while its objects behave incorrectly. For manipulation, matching what happens at contact matters as much as matching pixels.

Separately, a developer posting as pulpmatrix argued for source discipline around Video-to-Sim-to-Real claims circulating the same week:

Video-to-Sim-to-Real is real, documented in Google's Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics dev blog (MuJoCo twin, 87% ERQA). Cornhole isn't in it: no paper, no repo, no hit rate, and real throws calibrated the robot first.

Specialized vision-language-action systems such as OpenVLA-class policies, Physical Intelligence's π-family models, and NVIDIA GR00T with Isaac-oriented tooling optimize for action prediction under robot embodiments and typically rely on large teleoperation or simulation corpora. Scene-to-sim and generative world tools, World Labs-style reconstructions, NVIDIA DreamDojo-style action video, and Isaac Sim digital twins, emphasize environment synthesis or video prediction without necessarily owning the full control-and-QC loop shown in Google's prompts. Prior Google work such as Gemini Robotics-ER remains a related line for spatial perception and planning. For architecture reviews, the question is whether one frontier model plus heavy prompt harnesses displaces a pipeline of VLA, simulator, and labeler services.

Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions

In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios.

To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset "Nemotron-Personas-Japan." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).

This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development. The Nemotron-Personas collection, including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim, enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.

It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer. This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized:

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training:

Every persona is fully synthetic. No real individuals are represented, and the dataset is designed to reduce privacy risk. Demographics and household finances follow official statistics and public survey data, and names follow real Japanese naming patterns. Personas are built from these distributions, not from records about real people.

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI.

The release also serves anyone building for Japanese users. It holds 9M personas, 50% more than Nemotron-Personas-Japan, across 50 fields instead of 22. That gives any Japanese-language project finer slices of the population to train and test on.

The synthetic personas in this dataset can be leveraged for:

Access to diverse, high-quality training data that reflects real-world populations has long been a challenge in AI development. Enterprise AI development has predominantly relied on private data, creating barriers for researchers, startups, and particularly AI developers in regions with limited available data.

By releasing Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan under CC BY 4.0, we provide access to enterprise-grade, high-quality synthetic data, empowering anyone to build culturally grounded AI systems with lower cost and less privacy risk.

Nemotron-PII-Japan launches the same day. It holds 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, for training and testing detection and redaction models. Its documents are built on Nemotron-Personas-Japan. Use Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan to simulate customers, and Nemotron-PII-Japan to test how your pipeline protects their data.

You can download this dataset using the command below to help develop AI that genuinely understands Japanese culture and language.

Use cases for building production-ready applications:

From teams building AI in Japan to global developers aiming for broader regional deployment, Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan dataset provides the authentic, privacy-conscious foundation required for your applications.

MetricShell: How We Tried to Solve the Metrics Problem for Short-Lived Containers

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

I've heard this question come up many times over the years, and I've been involved in quite a few discussions about it myself: how do you collect metrics from an application running in a container if the application doesn't expose an HTTP /metrics endpoint?

Maybe it was never designed to do that. Or maybe adding an HTTP server just for monitoring feels like unnecessary overhead.

The question becomes particularly interesting when the application runs a short-lived task: a CLI command, a cron job, or a batch job.

One example I dealt with involved CLI commands in a PHP 7.4 monolith that we were gradually moving into a containerized environment.

The application already existed, did its job, and had years of development behind it. We needed both business metrics, such as counters and histograms, and technical metrics, such as database query execution times.

On physical or virtual servers, this was relatively straightforward. We could accumulate data in files, periodically aggregate it, and send it to the monitoring system.

A container starts, performs its task, and exits. There is no guarantee that Prometheus will perform its next scrape while the container is still running.

Even if the application can produce metrics, we still have a question: when exactly should they be collected, and who makes sure the final state remains available?

Imagine a cron command that finishes in five seconds while the Prometheus scrape interval is fifteen seconds.

Prometheus may never see that particular application instance.

We could send the metrics to a separate service. But that brings up another set of questions: who aggregates the data, how do we make sure the final update gets through, what happens with network delays, and who manages the metrics lifecycle?

What if the application exits with an error?

What if the container has already received a termination signal?

What if the monitoring infrastructure is temporarily unavailable?

What started as a simple request to "collect a few metrics" gradually turns into another service that somebody has to develop, deploy, and maintain.

All just to find out how many operations were processed, how long they took, and how much time the application spent querying the database.

Of course, we could simply stop collecting those metrics. But they're important to the application teams. Without them, it's much harder to understand what's happening inside the application.

And, as a tech lead, my conscience wouldn't let me casually throw away data that could become invaluable at the worst possible moment.

One of the first suggestions from the architecture committee was to write our own wrapper.

At first glance, that sounded reasonable: a small helper process that accepts metrics and exposes them to Prometheus.

Writing a prototype is one thing. Making it behave correctly inside a container is another.

You have to deal with termination signals, child processes, exit codes, time limits, application errors, and failures in the metrics-handling code itself.

And under no circumstances should monitoring interfere with the application's business logic or prevent it from completing its job.

The infrastructure team, meanwhile, wasn't enthusiastic about deploying additional components.

Kubernetes already had a working monitoring setup. Prometheus was scraping the microservices, everything was configured, and someone was maintaining it.

Why build another infrastructure layer just for a handful of cron jobs?

At some point, the discussion was essentially:

"The monolith can live without those metrics for now. Or spend the time adapting it to the new infrastructure."

But even adapting the application wouldn't solve the fundamental problem of short-lived processes.

You can teach a PHP application to expose /metrics. If it exits before the next scrape, Prometheus may still collect nothing.

Naturally, the first thing to do was look at how other people had already solved this problem.

For a long-running service, this is the obvious approach.

The application exposes /metrics, and Prometheus scrapes it periodically.

But with short-lived CLI processes, we run into the lifecycle problem again. The process may exit before the next scrape.

Pushgateway is an established option for certain batch-job scenarios.

The application pushes its metrics to Pushgateway, and Prometheus scrapes them from there.

However, Pushgateway has its own metrics lifecycle. Metrics can remain available after the application has finished, so their freshness and cleanup need to be managed explicitly.

It also introduces another infrastructure component and network communication with it.

For service-level batch jobs, Pushgateway may be exactly the right choice. But it isn't always a good fit for metrics associated with individual instances of short-lived workloads.

Another option is to write metrics to a file and expose them through Node Exporter.

For some workloads, this is a simple and effective solution.

But it requires an appropriate file-sharing arrangement and collection infrastructure. In a containerized environment, especially when job instances are created and removed dynamically, that raises additional questions.

We could run a separate exporter container alongside the application.

That separates the application's responsibilities from metrics exposition.

But it also adds a container, consumes resources, requires communication between the two processes, and makes their lifecycles something we need to coordinate.

OpenTelemetry offers a much broader set of capabilities for working with telemetry.

OpenTelemetry Collector can receive metrics from an application and expose them through an HTTP endpoint for Prometheus.

It can also run locally, even inside the same container, so a separate centralized service isn't strictly necessary.

However, the Collector primarily handles telemetry processing and delivery. It doesn't act as a ready-made supervisor for an arbitrary application process.

In our scenario, we would still need to implement the PHP process startup, signal forwarding, child-process cleanup, exit-code preservation, and a bounded wait for the final scrape after the workload finishes.

In other words, we could build the required behavior around OpenTelemetry Collector, but we'd still have to write and maintain our own wrapper.

As it turned out, that wrapper was precisely the part we wanted to make reusable.

All of these approaches are valid. In fact, any one of them might be the best solution for a particular workload.

But we wanted several properties at the same time:

Among the options we examined, we didn't find one that combined all of these properties without additional trade-offs.

I reached out to colleagues at other companies.

It turned out they had encountered similar situations.

And not necessarily with large monoliths. Sometimes it was an ordinary CLI application, a cron job, or a worker that ran its task and exited.

The workloads were different, but the underlying problem was familiar: the application should do its job, while the infrastructure should be able to collect metrics in the usual way.

During the research, I also used ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, and YandexGPT to discuss alternatives, challenge assumptions, and explore architectural ideas.

Of course, an LLM saying it hasn't seen a solution doesn't prove that such a solution doesn't exist. The research still had to rely on the documentation of existing tools, comparisons of their capabilities, and our actual requirements.

And gradually, the idea of a separate tool took shape.

Before writing any code, we needed to establish some boundaries.

There was no point in creating a replacement for existing tools.

If an application already exposes a proper Prometheus endpoint and runs long enough to be scraped regularly, it doesn't need another component.

If Pushgateway fits a particular batch-job scenario, use Pushgateway.

If the infrastructure is already built around OpenTelemetry, there's no reason to abandon it just to introduce something new.

A containerized workload that cannot, or should not, be responsible for exposing its own metrics to Prometheus.

Not bare metal. Not a general-purpose monitoring system. Not a new central metrics aggregator.

Just a container, its application, and the standard Prometheus pull model.

The idea was to place a small adapter directly inside the application container.

It would receive metrics locally, expose them on /metrics, and account for the workload's lifecycle.

No need to rework the application around a new monitoring architecture.

Once we had defined the scope, we could put together the basic requirements.

First. The application should start and finish just as it would without the wrapper.

Its exit code must be preserved. Signals must be forwarded correctly. Child processes must be handled and reaped.

Second. The application must be able to submit metrics locally, without communicating with external monitoring infrastructure.

Third. Metrics must be exposed through the standard HTTP /metrics endpoint, so Prometheus can scrape them.

Fourth. The application must be able to submit a complete snapshot of its metrics.

Fifth. For applications that don't want to build their own snapshots, there should be a simple way to work with counters, gauges, and histograms.

Sixth. After the application exits naturally, its final metrics should remain available for a limited time.

We cannot guarantee that Prometheus will collect those metrics if it's unavailable or hasn't discovered the container in time.

But we can give it another opportunity to scrape them without keeping the container alive indefinitely.

Finally, the whole thing should work inside a single container, with no mandatory additional infrastructure.

The result of this research and implementation was MetricShell.

Instead of making the application manage its own HTTP endpoint, we give that responsibility to a small wrapper process.

MetricShell starts as PID 1 inside the container and then launches the user's command.

That might be a PHP CLI application, a cron job, or a worker.

MetricShell supervises the process, receives metrics, and exposes them through /metrics.

Meanwhile, the application continues doing its actual job.

The plan looked straightforward: start up, accept some metrics, serve them over HTTP, and exit.

There's a law of software development that seems to apply here: the less time you expect something to take, the longer it actually takes.

Or how a couple of hours quietly turned into a couple of months.

And then there are the details of running as PID 1 on Linux: forwarding signals, dealing with child processes, making sure they're properly cleaned up, and preserving the application's actual exit code.

In the end, we had to design a proper state machine, define event ordering, and deal with races between process termination, metrics ingestion, and HTTP requests.

The hardest part of building a tool for metrics turned out to have very little to do with metrics.

It was about getting process termination right.

The current implementation supports two modes.

The application builds a complete snapshot of its metrics and submits it to MetricShell.

When a new valid snapshot is accepted, it atomically replaces the previous one.

This is useful when the application already collects its own metrics and can produce their complete state.

In this mode, MetricShell maintains a local metrics registry.

The application sends operations such as incrementing a counter, setting a gauge, or recording an observation in a histogram.

Communication takes place over a local Unix socket.

This means every application doesn't need to implement a full Prometheus registry of its own.

Both modes use the same mechanism for exposing metrics to Prometheus.

Imagine that our PHP command has finished processing its data.

Normally, once the main process exits, the container will soon terminate as well.

MetricShell, however, runs as PID 1 and supervises the application process.

When the workload exits naturally, MetricShell finalizes metrics ingestion, freezes the last valid state, and can continue serving it through /metrics.

What happens next depends on the configuration.

MetricShell can exit immediately, wait for a configured duration, or wait for a specified number of eligible completed scrape responses, subject to a finite timeout.

It then exits while preserving the workload's exit status, unless a higher-priority MetricShell-owned failure occurred.

So Prometheus gets another opportunity to collect the final metrics.

This is not guaranteed delivery, and it is not a replacement for durable storage.

But for this particular class of workloads, it allows us to stick with the familiar Prometheus pull model.

After the workload exits naturally, MetricShell can continue serving the frozen final snapshot until the configured wait condition is met or its timeout expires.

If Prometheus doesn't scrape the metrics in time, MetricShell still exits within the configured limits.

One important detail: this final-scrape waiting behavior applies to natural workload completion. If the container is externally terminated, MetricShell follows its bounded shutdown procedure, and the final wait may be interrupted.

At the time of writing, the current published release is v0.2.2.

MetricShell is written in Go, released under the MIT license, and supports Linux on amd64 and arm64.

You don't need to write an application just to see how it works.

A runnable example is published on GitHub Container Registry:

You'll see the metrics exposed by MetricShell.

To integrate it with your own application, there's also an artifact image containing the MetricShell binary, which you can copy into your application's Docker image.

This only illustrates how to integrate the wrapper. The application must still submit metrics through one of the supported local interfaces, and Prometheus must be configured to discover and scrape the container.

For production deployments, the documentation recommends pinning images by digest and using the documented configuration.

Docker and Kubernetes examples, protocols, configuration options, and operational limitations are available in the repository.

Every architectural decision comes with trade-offs.

It introduces another process inside the container and takes responsibility for supervising the workload correctly.

The application must still produce or publish its own metrics. MetricShell cannot magically figure out which business metrics should be measured.

The final snapshot is only available for a bounded period. If Prometheus misses that window, the metrics may be lost.

The metrics registry lives in the memory of a particular MetricShell instance. It does not restore its previous state after a restart.

MetricShell also doesn't handle Prometheus target discovery, time-series storage, or monitoring infrastructure configuration.

MetricShell solves a specific problem without trying to grow into an entire monitoring system.

At this point, the core functionality of MetricShell is implemented.

The source code, documentation, architectural decisions, and published artifacts are available on GitHub.

But one question remains: how useful is this approach to other engineers?

Maybe the existing tools are perfectly sufficient for most teams.

Maybe this problem comes up much more often than it seems.

Or maybe somebody has already solved it in a simpler and more elegant way.

If even three developers or DevOps engineers end up using MetricShell, or recommending it for a suitable scenario, I'll consider the project worthwhile.

After all, one of those three is already accounted for: me.

I'd be interested in technical criticism of the architecture, especially limitations I may have overlooked.

Technical discussions, corrections, and alternative approaches are welcome.

GitHub: https://github.com/Denki77/metricshell

Both colleagues and AI tools helped me throughout the research and implementation.

And, of course, thanks to everyone I discussed the monitoring of containerized workloads with.

Conversations like these are often where new engineering solutions begin.
