When Property, Fixture, and Flake Signals Disagree: A Precedence Table for Agent Patch Gates

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

A gate that averages three weak signals into one score will admit patches it should have held. The fix is not a better score. It is a fixed precedence order between channels that answer different questions, plus a resolver whose only job is to say which channel wins.

Below is a design for that resolver. It assumes you already collect three kinds of evidence for agent-authored patches: property checks over invariants, a content hash of your test fixtures, and a scoped freeze list for known-flaky tests. The code is illustrative — it was written for this article and has not been run against a real repository. The tables and the verification plan are the parts you can adopt directly.

Before any precedence matters, agree on what each channel can and cannot prove.

The failure mode this table prevents: an agent edits a fixture so a property passes, while an active freeze silences the one test that would have caught it. Each channel reports "fine" and the composition is not fine.

Resolve in four numbered steps, in this order, and stop at the first match.

Step 3 is where most gates go wrong: they treat a freeze as an acquittal. A freeze only means "this failure is not new information". If the base tree fails the same check, the freeze is masking a pre-existing problem and should be deleted, not extended.

The resolver reads three JSON files and prints one verdict plus reason codes. Prerequisites: Python 3.9+, a CI job that writes the three files, and an ISO date for today so runs are reproducible.

The exit-code mapping is a policy decision, not a technical one: many teams want hold to block merge while still allowing the pipeline to finish so the reviewer sees the reason codes. Pick one mapping and document it, or reviewers will read green builds as approvals.

A path-based check passes when the agent overwrites a fixture in place. Hash the content instead:

Two constraints keep this honest. First, the manifest must live outside the agent's write scope — otherwise the patch can rewrite both the fixture and the expected hash. Second, patch_declares_fixture_change must come from the patch's own diff, not from the agent's prose summary; parse the touched paths.

A freeze record needs three fields to be usable: a test id, an expiry date, and a recorded base-tree result. Without the base-tree field, step 3 cannot distinguish "flaky" from "broken on main since last month". Without the expiry, the freeze becomes permanent by inertia.

Two rules follow. Freezes never apply to tests added by the patch — a new test has no history, so it cannot be known-flaky. And an expired freeze must be deleted, not bumped; a date bump is a silent assertion that the flake is still tolerable.

The resolver is a decision function, so test it like one: synthetic evidence in, expected verdict out, one row per precedence rule. This is a plan, not a result — run it before trusting the gate.

Add one order check the table cannot express: feed a payload where fixture mutation and a property failure both occur, and assert the verdict is reject with the fixture reason only. If the resolver reports the property failure, your precedence is inverted somewhere.

Small projects often skip gates because the runner costs money or a credit card. MonkeyCode's free server option and free model access are relevant here — both are operator-supplied availability claims, so check current terms before depending on them. The useful split: run the resolver and a scratch base-tree checkout on the free server, and use free model access to draft candidate property invariants for review. Drafted invariants still need a seeded-bug check before admission, for the same reason tautological tests do.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

This design reconciles evidence; it cannot tell you whether an invariant is worth asserting. A well-run gate over vacuous properties will admit bad patches with a clean audit trail.

The fixture hash is only as strong as its write boundary. If the agent can edit the manifest, the channel is decorative. If your repository has no stable fixture set, hash nothing and say so — a channel that always reports clean teaches reviewers to ignore it.

Skip this if a human reads every diff before merge anyway, or if you have no base-tree checkout to compare against; the third rule is unimplementable without one. Start with rule 1 and rule 2 only, which need no base tree, and add the freeze attribution when the checkout exists.

The gate's value is that it disagrees in writing. Record the reason code next to the verdict, and the next reviewer can argue with the rule instead of with the agent.

null vs undefined in JavaScript: Differences, Checks and When to Use Each (Tested Examples)

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

Posted on Nov 9 • Originally published at mfaysal.com

undefined means a value was never assigned (missing property, missing argument, bare return). null is an intentional empty value you assign yourself. Prefer === when you care which one you have, use == null when either should count as empty, and reach for ?? / optional chaining when you want defaults without treating 0 or '' as missing.

MDN documents both primitives: null is the intentional absence of an object value, while undefined is the primitive for an uninitialized value. This guide shows the behaviour with real output from Node.js 24.22.1 running test/js/demo.mjs on this box. If loose vs strict equality still feels fuzzy, the null == undefined case below is one of the classic places where == and === disagree.

I also checked the same snippets mentally against everyday DOM and fetch patterns: document.getElementById returns null on a miss, optional JSON fields come back as undefined when absent, and many REST APIs send explicit null for cleared fields. Keeping those three stories straight saves a surprising number of production bugs.

Rule of thumb I use in application code: assign null when I want to say "I looked, there is nothing." Leave a property undefined (or omit it) when it was never set. Check with === null / === undefined when the difference matters, and with == null when either empty state should take the same branch.

The first surprise every JavaScript developer hits:

typeof null === "object" is a decades-old language quirk. It does not mean null is a real object you can read properties from. Accessing a property on null or undefined throws - the crash covered in Cannot read properties of undefined.

Use typeof to detect undefined. Detect null with value === null, not with typeof.

Loose equality treats them as matching. Strict equality does not:

Both are falsy, so if (!value) collapses them with 0, '' and false. That is often too aggressive. The idiom if (value == null) catches only null and undefined - useful when zero should still count as a real value. For a deeper look at loose vs strict equality, see == vs === in JavaScript.

A property you never set is undefined. A property you set to null is present and empty:

APIs often use null to mean "field exists but is empty" (no email on file) and omit the key - or leave it undefined after JSON.parse of a missing field - to mean "not provided". Pick one convention in your own code and stick to it. Object keys with an undefined value still show up in Object.keys if you assigned them explicitly:

This is one of the most practical differences in day-to-day functions:

Omitting the argument or passing undefined applies the default. Passing null does not - you get the string "null" after concatenation. If callers might send null from an API, normalize at the edge: name = name ?? "guest" inside the body, or reject null explicitly. Variables declared with let/const without an initializer are undefined until assigned; see var vs let vs const for the scoping side of that story.

Optional chaining short-circuits to undefined when it hits null or undefined, instead of throwing:

That return value is always undefined on a miss - never null - even if an intermediate was null. MDN's page on optional chaining covers ?.() and ?.[] forms too. Pair it with ?? when you want a default after a safe read.

?? only falls through for null and undefined. || falls through for every falsy value:

Use ?? when 0, '' or false are valid data. Use || only when any falsy value should become the default. MDN documents the operator under nullish coalescing.

JSON has null but no undefined. Serialization reflects that:

Object keys whose value is undefined are dropped. Array holes / undefined slots become null in the JSON text. After JSON.parse, a missing key reads back as undefined, while an explicit JSON null stays null. MDN's JSON.stringify page covers replacer behaviour if you need custom handling.

A function with no return yields undefined. Returning null is a deliberate choice:

Reading a variable that was never declared is a ReferenceError, not undefined - except with typeof, which safely returns "undefined":

Sparse arrays also produce undefined reads for empty slots, but in says the index is missing:

Three places this distinction shows up constantly:

Optional chaining helps for deep reads, but remember a miss always yields undefined, even when the chain hit a null. If you need to preserve an explicit null from an API as null in your UI state, assign it deliberately after the read instead of relying on ?. alone.

Array holes are another footgun: sparse slots read as undefined, yet in says the index is missing, and map skips the callback for empty slots. Prefer dense arrays (filter, flat, or explicit undefined fills) when you care about every index.

If you call something that is not a function while handling these values, you will see a different error - covered in TypeError: X is not a function.

Quick decision tree I use when reviewing a PR:

All snippets above were run on Node.js 24.22.1 via test/js/demo.mjs. The same results hold in current Chromium and Firefox for the language-level bits (typeof, ??, ?., JSON.stringify). DOM return values are browser APIs, not Node, but the null convention is the same in the HTML Standard.

undefined means a value was never assigned (missing property, missing argument, no return). null is an intentional empty value you assign. They compare equal with == and unequal with ===.

It is a long-standing language quirk. null is still a primitive, not a real object. Detect it with value === null, not with typeof.

When either null or undefined should take the same branch. value == null is true only for those two; it leaves 0, '' and false alone.

No. Defaults apply when the argument is missing or undefined. Passing null uses null as the value.

?? falls back only for null and undefined. || falls back for every falsy value, including 0, '' and false.

JSON has null but not undefined. JSON.stringify drops object keys whose value is undefined, and turns undefined array slots into null. JSON.parse of a missing key yields undefined when you read it.

Reading a missing property returns undefined. The key is not in the object. An explicit null means the key exists and was set empty.

It returns null, not undefined. That is a common DOM example of intentional emptiness, so check with === null or == null before you read properties.

UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable where it is not associated with a value in Python: 10 Causes and Fixes (Tested Examples)

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

Posted on Nov 9 • Originally published at mfaysal.com

Python raises UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'x' where it is not associated with a value when a function reads a name that Python has decided is local to that function, but the line that gives it a value has not run yet. Any assignment to a name anywhere inside a function (including +=, for, import, del and except ... as) makes that name local for the whole function. The usual fixes are to give the variable a value before any branch or loop, pass values in and return them, or declare global or nonlocal when you really mean an outer variable.

On Python 3.10 and older the same error reads UnboundLocalError: local variable 'x' referenced before assignment. It is the same problem with a friendlier message in newer versions. The Python docs list UnboundLocalError as a subclass of NameError, raised for a local variable that has no value bound to it yet.

The confusing part is that the variable often does exist, right at the top of the file. I hit it myself on my first visit counter. I reproduced every example below on Python 3.13.5, and I re-ran the first one on 3.10.22, 3.11.17, 3.14.8 and 3.15.0rc3 to compare the messages. Paths in the tracebacks point at my test scripts under /workspace/seo-posts-nov08/test/python/.

Here is the classic version: a module-level counter and a function that tries to bump it.

The carets point at count on the += line. Python 3.11.17, 3.14.8 and 3.15.0rc3 printed the same final message. Python 3.10.22 printed the older wording, UnboundLocalError: local variable 'count' referenced before assignment, without the caret lines. Same bug, same fixes.

Python decides the scope of every name when it compiles a function, before any line runs. The rule from the execution model is simple: if a name is bound anywhere in a function body, it is local to that whole function, unless you declare it global or nonlocal. Position does not matter. An assignment on the last line still makes the name local on the first line.

So count += 1 means "read local count, add 1, store local count". The read happens first, the local has no value yet, and Python refuses to quietly fall back to the global with the same name. That refusal is a good thing. A silent fallback would make bugs far harder to spot.

You can watch the compiler's decision yourself. This script inspects the function before calling it:

co_varnames and symtable both list total as local before the function runs. And because UnboundLocalError subclasses NameError, except NameError catches both.

Every cause below comes back to the same rule: something assigns the name inside the function, and a read runs before that assignment. Use this table to jump to the one that matches your code.

This is the example from the top of the post, and it is the most common cause by far. Counters, running totals and "last seen" values all hit it. +=, -=, *= and friends all count as assignments, so the name becomes local.

The cleanest fix is to stop mutating the global at all: pass the value in and return the new one. If the function really must change module-level state, declare it with the global statement. Here are both, plus the fixes for causes 3, 4 and 6, from one test run:

I prefer the return-value version: it keeps functions easy to test.

This one surprises people because the failing line is a plain read. The assignment that causes it sits further down:

The traceback points at the print, not at total = 0. Whenever the caret lands on a harmless-looking read, scan the rest of the function for any assignment to the same name. Usually you meant a different variable, so rename the local (for example new_total = 0). If you really meant to reset the global, add global total as the first line of the function.

Here the function works for some inputs and crashes for others, which makes it easy to ship by accident:

A score of 72 takes the if branch and returns "pass". A score of 30 skips the only assignment, so result never gets a value. The fix is to set a default before the branch (result = "fail") or add an else. The fixes run above prints label: pass fail.

A close cousin of this bug is a function that only returns inside an if. That one does not raise UnboundLocalError. It quietly returns None, and the crash shows up later as 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable.

A for loop assigns its target on every pass. If the iterable is empty, the loop body never runs and the name never gets a value:

Two items work fine. An empty list crashes. Give the name a value before the loop, as last_item(items, default=None) does in the fixes run, or skip the loop entirely and use items[-1] if items else None. Empty lists cause plenty of other crashes too. If you also index into them, see IndexError: list index out of range.

This is a nasty one, because the second error hides the first. open() fails, so f is never assigned, and then finally tries to close it:

The handler ran and printed its message, then f.close() blew up. For files, sockets and locks, a with block solves this completely: it only closes what actually opened. When you cannot use with, set the variable to None before the try and check it in finally. Here are the with version and the fixes for causes 9 and 10:

Closures follow the same rule. The inner function assigns count, so count is local to the inner function, even though the outer function already has one:

The fix is nonlocal, which tells Python to bind the name in the nearest enclosing function scope. In the fixes run, the counter with nonlocal n printed nonlocal: 1 2 3. The official Python programming FAQ covers this exact case under "Why am I getting an UnboundLocalError when the variable has a value?".

global would be wrong here: it points at the module, not at make_counter.

del unbinds a name. Inside a function, the name stays local, so reading it afterwards raises the same error:

This usually appears after a refactor adds a del above an older use. Move the del after the last use, or drop it; locals are freed when the function returns anyway.

import json is an assignment too: it binds the name json. Put one inside a function, even in a branch that never runs, and the module-level import stops working for that whole function:

The same thing happens with from x import y and with any name that matches a module you imported at the top. Keep imports at the top of the file, or put a lazy import at the very start of the function.

Python deletes the name bound by except ... as err when the handler finishes. The compound statements reference explains why: it breaks a reference cycle between the exception and the stack frame. Inside a function, reading err afterwards fails:

At module level the same code raises NameError instead. Either way, copy the exception to another variable inside the handler (last_error = err), as the fixes run above shows. It printed last error was: ValueError("invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'").

Built-ins follow the rule as well. Assign to len, list, id, type or sum anywhere in a function, and every earlier use of that built-in in the function breaks:

The error says "local variable 'len'", which looks bizarre until you spot the assignment two lines down. Rename the variable (word_count) and the built-in works again. If you are cleaning up text or JSON while you debug, my free browser tools run entirely on your device. Pylint (redefined-builtin) and Ruff with its flake8-builtins rules flag shadowed built-ins before you run the code.

Python decided at compile time that the name is local to the function, because something in the function assigns to it. Then a line read the name before that assignment had run, so the local had no value.

Yes. Python 3.10 and older print local variable 'x' referenced before assignment. Python 3.11 and newer print cannot access local variable 'x' where it is not associated with a value. In my tests the cause and fixes were identical.

Any assignment to the same name inside the function, including +=, makes it a separate local variable for the whole function. The module-level variable is ignored until you declare it with global.

Use global only when the function genuinely must change module-level state. In most code it is cleaner to pass the value in as an argument and return the new value.

global binds the name at module level. nonlocal binds it in the nearest enclosing function, which is what you need for counters inside closures and decorators.

Yes. issubclass(UnboundLocalError, NameError) returned True in my test, so except NameError catches both. Fixing the scope is still better than catching the error.

The Model May Draft the Happy Path; Humans Own Every Absence Claim

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

A model drafting documentation from a repository describes what exists far better than what does not, because the code is a positive artifact: routes, flags, and types are visible, while "this endpoint rejects batched writes" exists only in someone's head. That asymmetry is the practical failure you have to design around, and it does not go away with a bigger model or a longer prompt. The control that works in my experience is narrow and mechanical: let the model draft the happy path freely, then force every absence, limit, and guarantee claim into a review queue where a named human signs it.

This article describes that two-layer control, gives an illustrative scanner you can adapt, and states plainly where the approach breaks down. The script below was written for this article and has not been executed against a real docs tree, so treat the pattern list as a starting point rather than a validated classifier.

Positive claims about an API surface degrade gracefully: a stale field name is visibly wrong to anyone who opens the source file. Negative claims degrade silently, because nothing in the codebase contradicts a sentence like "the worker does not retry on 5xx" until an incident proves it. A model asked to be helpful will also fill gaps in a plausible direction, adding cautions that sound responsible but were never verified. Those invented caveats are worse than missing ones, since a reader may plan an architecture around a limitation that does not exist.

The categories that need human ownership are small but high-leverage: absences ("does not", "unsupported"), scope limits ("only works with", "at most"), deprecation timelines, and behavioral guarantees ("idempotent", "thread-safe", "atomic"). Everything else, including most of the prose, examples, and parameter walkthroughs, can stay model-drafted with normal review.

Before any prose generation, give the model an explicit ownership contract and require it to flag the sentences it cannot ground. The contract below is illustrative text you can paste into a system prompt; the key part is that the model must emit a placeholder rather than a confident sentence.

The placeholder is deliberately invalid, so it can never pass a merge check, and it is also greppable. Models under-report their own uncertainty, however, so the prompt layer is a convenience rather than a guarantee. That is why the second layer is mechanical.

The scanner ignores what the model claimed about itself and looks only at the text. It skips fenced code blocks and inline code so that flags like --no-cache do not register as absence claims, then classifies each remaining sentence into the four categories.

Hitting hCaptcha in 2026: What Developers Can Still Use

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

NoneCap is an hCaptcha solving API for developers: send a sitekey and page URL, get a token back. nonecap.com

NoneCap is an hCaptcha solving API for developers: send a sitekey and page URL, get a token back. nonecap.com

NoneCap is an hCaptcha solving API for developers: send a sitekey and page URL, get a token back. nonecap.com

If your scraper or test suite stopped at an hCaptcha widget sometime in the last two years, the service you used to send it to may be part of the problem.

2Captcha removed hCaptcha from its API documentation around the start of 2025. CapSolver's hCaptcha documentation page has returned a 404 since January 2025. If your code was written against either one for hCaptcha, you need a different place to send those jobs.

This post covers how token-based solving works, what to do when the site is yours, and one way to wire a solver into a script.

If the hCaptcha widget sits on an app you control and you only need your end-to-end tests to get past it, you don't need a solving service. hCaptcha publishes test keys for this. In your test environment, set the widget's sitekey to 10000000-ffff-ffff-ffff-000000000001 and your server's secret to the matching test secret from hCaptcha's docs. The widget then passes without a challenge and siteverify accepts the dummy token, so your CI never depends on a third party.

Everything below is for sites you don't control: a scraper collecting public data, a monitoring job, or a test that runs against a staging environment someone else owns.

When a person solves an hCaptcha, the widget gets back a token that starts with P1_. The page puts it in a hidden form field called h-captcha-response (or hands it to a JavaScript callback), and the site's backend checks it with hCaptcha's siteverify endpoint before it lets the request through.

A token-based solver gives you that same token without a browser on your side. The flow has four steps:

Two details trip people up. A token is single use and expires after about two minutes, so request it right before you submit, not at the start of a long job. And some sites check that the browser submitting the token matches the one that earned it, so send the User-Agent the solver returns with the token.

NoneCap is a hosted API that only handles hCaptcha, including invisible widgets and enterprise sitekeys that carry rqdata. You send a sitekey and a URL and get a token back. Failed solves aren't charged.

The wait parameter (1 to 90 seconds) holds the request open until the solve finishes. If it's still running when the window closes, you get a 202 with a null token, and you poll GET /v1/solves/{id} until the status is solved, failed or expired.

The same call from Node 18+, with no SDK:

In Playwright or Puppeteer, you'd read the sitekey from the page, make this call, write the token into the h-captcha-response textarea (plus the g-recaptcha-response compatibility field if the page has one), then submit the form or fire the widget's callback for invisible sitekeys.

One more thing helps over time. A token can pass hCaptcha and still be refused by the site that asked for it. When that happens, report the solve ID to POST /v1/feedback with "outcome": "rejected". It's the only way the service learns that a site turned a token down.

You may not need to rewrite anything. NoneCap has compatibility endpoints for both request formats:

The full API reference, with cURL and Go examples alongside the ones above, is at nonecap.com/api-reference. There are integration guides for Selenium, Playwright, Puppeteer, Scrapy and Go at nonecap.com/solutions, and a plain-text version of all the docs for coding assistants at nonecap.com/llms.txt.

Among other things, launching AIModels.fyi ... Find the right AI model for your project - https://aimodels.fyi

Among other things, launching AIModels.fyi ... Find the right AI model for your project - https://aimodels.fyi

TurnWise applies turn-level Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to streaming video, where a model repeatedly chooses to answer or wait as new frames arrive. Its central claim is specific: silence-completed prefix scoring estimates each decision’s group-relative remaining return, so a later reply is not trained using rewards earned before that decision.

The problem is that standard trajectory-level GRPO broadcasts one advantage across every turn. A redundant reply after an early success can inherit positive credit, while a useful follow-up after earlier failures can inherit negative credit. TurnWise separates the return from each turn onward from the reward already accrued, then weights response and waiting turns equally in the policy loss.

The method is evaluated on ProactiveVQA, OVO-Timing, and StreamingBench using Qwen2.5-VL-3B and Qwen3-VL-4B backbones. The authors report the best aggregate scores on all three benchmarks with both models, and say that turn-mean aggregation improves response timing while reducing repetition relative to credit-only optimization. A related video-RL direction emphasizes focused video reasoning, whereas TurnWise focuses on when to respond during a stream.

Streaming interaction differs from offline video question answering because the model acts on partial observations and must account for what it has already told the user. A response can be timely and useful at one point, while another response at a later decision adds no information. The learning signal therefore needs to reflect both answer quality and the timing of each response-or-wait choice.

The paper positions TurnWise against MMDuet2, ThinkStream, and StreamPro, which improve interaction rewards or assess response-level and trajectory-level quality. It argues that these reward designs still leave a key GRPO issue: a single trajectory advantage is shared across turns. TurnWise changes credit assignment and loss weighting rather than introducing a new trajectory reward. The broader distinction between shared sequence feedback and per-step credit also appears in turn-level credit assignment, although TurnWise applies it to streaming video response and waiting decisions.

The concrete failure case is a trajectory with a successful early answer followed by a redundant reply: the later action may still receive positive shared credit. The reverse can happen when a useful follow-up follows earlier failures. The authors’ correction subtracts group-relative accrued reward before each decision, allowing later turns to be judged by their remaining return.

Illustrative dialogue and advantage plot contrasting shared GRPO credit with TurnWise credit across turns.

The example contrasts a shared trajectory advantage with TurnWise’s remaining-return credit, showing how a later redundant reply can inherit earlier success under GRPO. The distinction motivates turn-specific learning signals.

For each sampled trajectory, TurnWise keeps the first t actions and replaces every later action with silence, then scores that prefix with the same observation plan and evaluation horizon. The difference between this score and the full trajectory score gives the return from turn t onward. Group-relative normalization produces a turn-specific advantage without a learned critic. The remaining-return construction is related in granularity to Turn-PPO advantage estimation, but TurnWise derives its signal from silence-completed video prefixes.

The prefix scores reuse the existing trajectory evaluations: the authors state that a silent suffix changes neither retained responses nor their preceding replies. This avoids additional rollouts and judge calls. A limitation of the method’s credit signal is that it depends on the fixed trajectory scorer, including its response-quality, timing, repetition, and out-of-window penalties.

TurnWise also changes the GRPO objective. It averages token losses within each turn and then averages across turns, so a long textual answer does not outweigh a short waiting action merely because it contains more tokens. The two mechanisms address separate issues: remaining-return advantages determine what credit a turn receives, while turn-mean aggregation determines how much that turn contributes to optimization.

TurnWise pipeline from streaming inputs and sampled trajectories to turn advantages and turn-mean loss.

The overview connects silence-completed prefix scoring to group-relative remaining-return advantages, then applies turn-mean aggregation. It summarizes how TurnWise aligns credit and policy weighting with streaming decisions.

Training starts from supervised fine-tuning on 100,874 instruction examples, then uses 3,983 streaming instances with groups of four sampled trajectories. The reward is PAUC-based and judged by gpt-oss-20b; the evaluation covers proactive answer quality, event-triggered timing, and real-time visual understanding. The paper reports one epoch of RL training for each configuration.

The named RL comparisons are MMDuet2, ThinkStream, and StreamPro, implemented in the same streaming GRPO framework, alongside the supervised models. TurnWise achieves the best aggregate scores on ProactiveVQA, OVO-Timing, and StreamingBench for both Qwen backbones. The supplied paper text does not include the numerical benchmark scores, so the size of its gains cannot be quantified here. A related line of work also studies turn-level credit policy optimization, while the comparisons reported here are MMDuet2, ThinkStream, and StreamPro.

The authors also report a component-level result: turn-mean aggregation improves response timing and reduces repetition compared with credit-only optimization. This supports their claim that turn-specific credit alone does not fix length-dependent weighting. The paper text provided does not specify a numerical repetition reduction or timing improvement.

TurnWise’s technical contribution is the pairing of silence-completed prefix scoring with turn-mean policy optimization. The first removes earlier accrued reward from a decision’s group-relative signal; the second gives each sampled response-or-wait decision equal loss weight. Both operate within GRPO and use the existing rollout group rather than a critic or extra trajectories.

The reported evidence is broad across three streaming benchmarks and two Qwen backbones, but the supplied results section gives aggregate rankings rather than score tables. It also does not provide the numerical gains, per-category results, or detailed ablation values. Those omissions limit how precisely a reader can compare effect sizes from the available text.

The paper’s stated edge case is the mismatch between trajectory quality and individual turn quality: a good trajectory can contain a bad turn, and a poor trajectory can contain a useful one. TurnWise is designed to address that mismatch under the paper’s PAUC-based scorer and streaming setup. Its reported findings do not establish performance beyond the listed benchmarks and configurations. Unlike difficulty-aware video RL, which targets video generation, TurnWise evaluates streaming video understanding and interaction timing.

This is a Plain English Papers summary of a research paper called Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit.

TokenPulse: Building the Leadership Team Behind Cost-Efficient AI Inference

As artificial intelligence (AI) moves from model training into large-scale production, inference computing is becoming an increasingly important factor in the economics of AI infrastructure. Inference demand is climbing alongside: the global AI infrastructure market is projected to grow from $982 billion in 2025 to $1.98 trillion by 2027, doubling in size over the two-year period. Companies deploying AI applications face rising inference costs, demanding real-time latency requirements, and the challenge of scaling their platforms as traffic grows.

In this environment, access to GPUs alone is no longer sufficient. The more difficult task is turning available computing capacity into reliable, cost-efficient token output at scale. Doing so requires not only advanced hardware and software optimization, but also the infrastructure partnerships, operational expertise, and commercial relationships needed to support growing demand.

This is the challenge that TokenPulse, a next-generation AI inference infrastructure company headquartered in San Francisco and Singapore, is seeking to address. Following the opening of its Asia-Pacific Operating Hub in Singapore, the company is bringing together data-center resources, GPU infrastructure, optimized inference engines, and globally coordinated serving capabilities to support AI workloads across regions.

Beyond its technology strategy, TokenPulse is placing considerable emphasis on the leadership team responsible for putting that infrastructure into operation. With backgrounds spanning data centers, government, investment, cloud engineering, and enterprise commercialization, its executives bring different capabilities to the increasingly complex business of AI inference.

At the center of TokenPulse's infrastructure strategy is Chairman Thomas Pang, whose more than 30 years of executive experience span government, investment, infrastructure, and corporate leadership.

Pang spent over two decades with Keppel, including serving as CEO of Keppel's Data Centres & Networks Division from 2014 to 2024. In that role, he oversaw the group's global data-center portfolio and digital connectivity businesses, gaining experience in the infrastructure development and partnerships that underpin large-scale computing operations.

That background is particularly relevant as TokenPulse expands its presence in Southeast Asia. While GPU performance and software efficiency remain central to AI inference, the ability to secure suitable data-center capacity, coordinate regional infrastructure resources, and establish long-term partnerships can be equally important to commercial delivery.

From its Singapore operating hub, TokenPulse is developing infrastructure relationships across Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and the wider region. Singapore also serves as a strategic link between North America's AI technology and customer ecosystems and Southeast Asia's expanding data-center and energy resources.

Pang's experience across public-sector engagement, investment, and infrastructure development provides a foundation for navigating these regional relationships. Rather than viewing computing capacity as a standalone resource, TokenPulse's strategy depends on coordinating infrastructure availability with the technical and commercial requirements of AI applications.

“Singapore is a natural choice for building our APAC operating hub, given its mature data center ecosystem, strong network connectivity, and deep talent pool,” said Pang. “Our foundations are rooted in decades of experience across data centers, networking, & cloud computing. Drawing on that experience in building and operating infrastructure at scale, we will continue investing in compute capacity and ecosystem support, delivering the best performance at the lowest cost per token.”

His comments reflect a broader challenge facing inference infrastructure providers: translating data-center resources into computing services that can meet the performance, cost, and reliability expectations of global AI customers.

Securing physical infrastructure is only one part of the equation. The efficiency of the software running on that infrastructure also determines how effectively GPU capacity can be converted into useful AI output.

CTO John Liu leverages 13 years of AI/ML infrastructure and Microsoft Azure experience to lead the optimization of the company's inference engine. His work allows enterprises to lower the costs of demanding AI models without sacrificing performance.

TokenPulse uses technologies including context parallelism and multi-tier key-value (KV) caching through HiCache to reduce repeated computation and improve serving performance.

According to the company's reported results, its cluster-level cache hit rate can reach 95%, while context parallelism has enabled up to a 75% reduction in 99th-percentile time to first token (P99 TTFT) compared with the same workload without context parallelism enabled. Actual performance improvements vary depending on workload and operating conditions.

These engineering capabilities illustrate how inference economics depends on more than GPU specifications. Effective software optimization can help businesses extract greater value from existing computing resources, making technical expertise an important part of TokenPulse's commercial strategy.

Matthew Rix, Senior Vice President of AI Infrastructure and Strategic Partnerships, brings over 20 years of data-center and cloud partnerships experience to TokenPulse. Leveraging a background that includes building a $90 million of DGX SuperPod pipeline with NVIDIA, Dell and IBM, he leads TokenPulse’s AI infrastructure strategy and strategic alliances.

As AI inference workloads expand, infrastructure providers must consider not only access to advanced GPUs, but also how hardware can be deployed, supported, and scaled across different operating environments.

Rix's background helps connect these infrastructure requirements with practical deployment planning and commercial partnerships. TokenPulse's roadmap includes the deployment of latest-generation NVIDIA AI infrastructure as part of its broader capacity expansion strategy.

Together with Pang's infrastructure expertise and Liu's engineering work, this adds another layer to the company's approach: aligning physical capacity, hardware deployment, and software efficiency rather than treating them as separate priorities.

Building an efficient inference platform also requires a clear understanding of how businesses intend to use it.

Senior Vice President Mazhar Hussain is a former Google executive drawing on 18 years of experience in AI and cloud, including partner ecosystem development with Microsoft, Meta, and NVIDIA, which drove over $1 billion in growth. He leverages this background to connect TokenPulse's technical infrastructure with commercial demand from global enterprises and AI platforms.

Different customer groups have different requirements for inference capacity. Some developers need flexible access while testing applications, while established enterprise customers may require more predictable performance, dedicated infrastructure, or longer-term capacity arrangements.

Understanding these differences is an important part of translating technical capabilities into services that customers can adopt and expand over time.

Hussain's commercial background complements the company's engineering and infrastructure capabilities by helping connect its computing platform with the expectations of global AI customers and strategic partners.

CEO Steven Zhou, a serial entrepreneur with over 20 years of experience scaling businesses across the U.S. and Asia, drives TokenPulse's overarching corporate strategy alongside CFO Mark Lu. They align capital planning and long-term investment to sustain expansion in the highly infrastructure-intensive AI industry.

Together, the leadership team's experience supports TokenPulse's approach to AI inference: combining infrastructure access, software optimization, hardware partnerships, and enterprise commercialization within a single business model.

That approach is reflected in the company's flexible consumption options, built around the principle of “Start small. Scale without replatforming.”

Customers can access computing capacity through three models on a unified technology stack:

●      Serverless (Pay per Token): API-based access for model evaluation, rapid deployment, and variable workloads.

●      On-Demand (Pay per GPU-Hour): Dedicated computing resources for customers requiring greater control and predictable performance.

●      Reserved Capacity: Contracted infrastructure capacity for sustained workloads and more customized requirements.

TokenPulse also offers managed cloud, Private VPC, and Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) deployment options to accommodate different operational and infrastructure needs.

The intention is to allow customers to begin with smaller AI workloads and expand their computing requirements without having to rebuild their platforms as their applications grow.

For businesses evaluating inference providers, that flexibility can matter as much as raw computing performance. Infrastructure availability, cost efficiency, deployment options, and the ability to support long-term growth all influence whether AI applications can scale successfully.

TokenPulse's strategy brings these considerations together, with its multidisciplinary leadership team providing the experience needed to address challenges at different stages of the infrastructure value chain.

As competition in AI inference increasingly shifts from GPU ownership toward efficient and reliable token delivery, the ability to coordinate technology, infrastructure, partnerships, and commercial execution may become an important differentiator.

For TokenPulse, the opening of its Singapore hub represents one part of that broader effort. Its longer-term challenge will be turning the combined expertise of its leadership team into scalable inference services that can meet the evolving demands of the global AI market.

TokenPulse is a next-generation AI inference infrastructure company headquartered in San Francisco and Singapore. The company combines latest-generation GPU infrastructure, an optimized inference engine, and global AI infrastructure capabilities to deliver high-performance, cost-efficient compute for foundation model companies, AI platforms, enterprises, and AI-native applications worldwide.

From Raw Sensor Signals to Regulatory-Grade Data: How Air Quality Monitoring Networks Are Engineered

📅 2026-11-09  |  Read Source →

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Air quality monitoring looks like a data problem: put a sensor on a pole, read a number, plot it. In practice, it is an engineering problem. The signal you get from a gas or particulate sensor is shaped by temperature, humidity, ageing materials and other gases in the air. Turning that raw signal into data that an environmental manager can defend in front of a regulator takes calibration, quality control, and a well-designed data pipeline.

This article walks through how modern air quality monitoring networks are built, from the physics of the sensor to the API that feeds your dashboards.

A low-power electrochemical or optical sensor does not measure “NO₂” or “PM2.5” directly. It produces a voltage or a light-scattering response, and software converts that into a concentration. Three effects make that conversion unreliable if left unmanaged:

None of these problems means air quality sensors are unusable. They mean the raw output cannot be trusted by itself, and that the quality of the data depends on everything done around the sensing element. These limitations are also documented in a 2019 review of low-cost sensor performance.

Regulatory reference stations are the benchmark. They use certified analysers, controlled shelters and trained operators, and they produce the data that legal limits are checked against. They are also expensive to install and maintain, so a city or an industrial site usually has very few of them.

That creates a coverage gap. Pollution is highly local: a road junction, a loading dock or a stockpile can have a very different profile from a station a kilometre away. Dense networks of compact monitors address this in three ways:

Spatial coverage: more measurement points per unit area show gradients that a single station cannot.

Response time: continuous, short-interval readings from the source area allow alerts within minutes rather than reports after the fact.

Cost of deployment: smaller units with lower power needs can be installed on existing infrastructure, which makes it practical to monitor a fence line or a port perimeter.

The two approaches are complementary. Reference stations anchor the network’s accuracy, and denser monitoring shows where, and when, to look more closely.

Near-reference sensors are not a different physical principle. They are the result of a disciplined process applied to the same sensing technologies. The main steps are:

Professional-grade air quality monitors such as Kunak AIR Pro are designed around exactly this chain, which is why they are discussed as near-reference instruments rather than simple indicators. Ultimately, data quality depends less on any single component than on how consistently the whole calibration and validation process is applied across the fleet and over time.

Accurate readings are only useful if they reach the right people and systems reliably. A typical IoT environmental monitoring architecture has four layers:

A dedicated air quality data platform such as Kunak AIR Cloud covers this chain in one place. The design principle holds for any stack, however: treat the measurement and the software as one system. If the cloud layer cannot trace a value back to its calibration state and QA flags, the numbers lose much of their value as evidence.

“Accurate” is not a useful specification on its own. Several frameworks define what performance is expected, and in which context:

CEN/TS 17660: This European technical specification sets out performance evaluation for air quality sensor systems, in separate parts for gases and particulate matter. Class 1 is the most demanding tier, intended for sensor systems that can be used for indicative measurements.

MCERTS for indicative monitors: The UK Environment Agency’s MCERTS scheme includes certification for indicative ambient monitors, giving buyers independent assurance beyond the manufacturer’s own claims.

US EPA performance targets: The EPA publishes performance targets and testing guidance for air sensors used in supplemental and informational monitoring, with metrics such as precision, bias, linearity and error. Its Air Sensor Toolbox is a good starting point for evaluation protocols.

Independent evaluations: Public test programmes, such as the South Coast AQMD’s AQ-SPEC, compare sensor performance in field and laboratory conditions and are useful for cross-checking any claim.

The regulatory context is also moving. The EU’s Ambient Air Quality Directive 2024/2881 tightens limit values for 2030, bringing them closer to the WHO’s 2021 Global Air Quality Guidelines. For PM2.5, for example, the annual EU limit value drops to 10 µg/m³, while the WHO guideline is 5 µg/m³. Tighter limits mean smaller margins, and smaller margins make measurement uncertainty and good documentation more important. Member states are also expected to make better use of supplementary methods to improve spatial coverage, which opens a clearer role for well-characterised sensor networks alongside reference stations.

For teams comparing options, certification is a practical filter. For example, Kunak AIR Pro is certified under MCERTS as an indicative ambient particulate monitor for PM2.5 and PM10 (certificate CSA MC230418/00), and the manufacturer reports alignment with the Class 1 criteria of CEN/TS 17660. The point is not the product, it is that this kind of independent evidence is what separates a monitoring network from a collection of sensors.

Different sectors use the same technology for different questions:

Industrial fenceline monitoring: Monitors placed around a plant boundary show whether emissions reach neighbouring areas, and combined with wind data, they help identify the source of an episode.

Ports: Ship traffic, cargo handling and trucks create overlapping sources. Distributed monitoring helps separate them and supports mitigation planning.

Mining and quarries: Dust is the main concern. Real-time particulate data lets operators adjust watering, blasting schedules or haulage before limits are exceeded.

Cities: Dense networks complement reference stations to map hotspots near schools, traffic corridors or low-emission zones, and to evaluate the impact of mobility policies.

Data centers: Gaseous contaminants and particulates can affect equipment reliability, and indoor and perimeter monitoring supports facility management and audits.

Before choosing hardware, it helps to answer the following questions:

What is the decision? Compliance reporting, operational control and public information need different levels of data quality.

Which pollutants and averaging periods matter? Match them to the applicable regulation or permit.

What evidence of performance exists? Look for third-party certification, published co-location results, and independent evaluations, not just datasheets.

How is calibration maintained? Ask whether baseline and span corrections can be applied remotely, and how often they are verified.

How are data quality and traceability handled? You should be able to see which readings were validated, flagged, or corrected, and why.

How does the data leave the platform? Check the API, protocols (4G, Ethernet, Modbus), and compatibility with your SCADA, BI, or reporting tools.

What is the siting plan? Height, distance to sources, wind patterns, and power availability all affect representativeness.

Who owns the process? Assign responsibility for maintenance, data review, and escalation before the first unit is installed.

Air quality data only becomes useful when its limits are understood and managed. Teams that treat monitoring as an engineering system, covering the sensor, the calibration, the pipeline and the standards, end up with data they can act on and defend.
